title: G7 Warns Iran to Stop Arming Houthis as Yemen Fighting Displaces 120,000
summary:
Seven of the world's most powerful countries have a blunt message for Iran: stop giving weapons to the Houthis in Yemen.

In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States said Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis. The G7 also condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia "in the strongest terms," calling the recent escalation a threat to regional and global energy security.

The timing matters. The statement came just before the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to speak. Iran has repeatedly denied supplying weapons to the Houthis, saying it only supports them politically.

So what's actually happening on the ground? Earlier this month, the Houthis — who already controlled most of Yemen's populated areas — seized Bab al-Mandab, a narrow maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden. It's one of the world's most important shipping routes. Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days, and the UN estimates more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the surge in fighting along the Red Sea coast.

Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government, has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes. The Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi cities and infrastructure, including the capital, Riyadh. In one attack, two children and a woman were killed, and eight others were injured.

The G7 called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions" and return to the political process "in good faith." The ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to Yemen's unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.

Meanwhile, the UK said it will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia — a single British Voyager aircraft based at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the move followed a Saudi request for military support, agreed on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. A diplomatic source told AFP that France has also pledged support, describing it as a "strictly defensive approach" to securing Saudi energy infrastructure.
why_it_matters: Yemen sits beside one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, so fighting there affects oil prices, cargo costs and food supplies far beyond the region — and the number of displaced families keeps growing. The episode also shows how a single joint statement can pull several great powers, and their militaries, deeper into someone else's civil war.

keywords.explanation: A group of seven major economies — the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States — whose governments coordinate on big global issues.
An armed movement that took over much of northern Yemen, including the capital, and now fights Yemen's internationally recognised government.
A narrow passage that ships must squeeze through, so blocking it can disrupt trade for the whole world.
Forced to leave home because of fighting or disaster, usually without knowing when you can return.
A country's right to govern itself and control its own territory without outside interference.
Refuelling a plane while it is flying, from a tanker aircraft, so it can stay in the air much longer.

background_read: The G7 (a group of seven major economies — the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States — whose governments coordinate on global policy) often issues joint statements to pressure other states, but the group has no army of its own, so its words matter only if member countries act. The statement was timed for the annual UN General Assembly (the September gathering in New York where leaders of nearly every country give speeches), which gives such warnings a large audience.

Yemen (a country at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula) has been in civil war since the Houthis — a movement that seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 — pushed the internationally recognised government out of much of the north. In 2015, a Saudi-led coalition began air strikes aimed at restoring that government, and the conflict has since become one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with millions dependent on aid.

Bab al-Mandab is a narrow strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. Ships travelling between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal must pass it, so a large share of global cargo and oil shipments depends on those waters staying open; that is why the G7 frames Houthi attacks as a threat to global energy security. Iran and Saudi Arabia are regional rivals that have backed opposing sides in several Middle Eastern conflicts, which is the deeper reason Iran's support for the Houthis worries Western governments.

RAF Akrotiri (a British military base on the island of Cyprus) gives the UK a permanent air presence in the eastern Mediterranean, which is why a single Voyager tanker aircraft can be deployed from there — a small, 'strictly defensive' contribution that France has reportedly also offered.
Article_Structure: LEAD: blunt one-line demand — seven powerful countries tell Iran to stop arming the Houthis
├─ WHO SIGNED: foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States
├─ DEMAND: Iran must 'end its arming of and support' for the Houthis
├─ CONDEMNATION: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia 'in the strongest terms' — a threat to regional and global energy security
└─ TIMING: issued just before the UN General Assembly, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak
COUNTER-CLAIM: Iran repeatedly denies supplying weapons, saying it supports the Houthis only politically
├─ STRATEGIC SEIZURE: the Houthis took Bab al-Mandab, where the southern Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden — one of the world's most important shipping routes
├─ HUMAN COST: thousands of refugees have fled; the UN estimates more than 120,000 Yemenis displaced by fighting along the Red Sea coast
├─ RETALIATION: Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government, has launched hundreds of air strikes
└─ CASUALTIES: Houthi drones and missiles hit Saudi cities and infrastructure including Riyadh; one attack killed two children and a woman and injured eight others
├─ Houthis to 'immediately cease all military actions'
├─ Return to the political process 'in good faith'
└─ Reaffirmed commitment to Yemen's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity

MILITARY BACKING: UK offers 'defensive air-to-air refuelling' — one Voyager aircraft at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus, following a Saudi request; France reportedly pledges a 'strictly defensive' contribution too
OPEN QUESTION: can outside pressure actually cut the flow of weapons and end the fighting, or does it widen the war?

perspectives.description: Supporters of the G7 statement argue that only collective pressure can shift Iran's behaviour, and that publicly naming the arms pipeline makes it harder to hide. The UK and France frame their support as narrowly defensive — refuelling aircraft to protect Saudi energy sites and Red Sea shipping — which, they say, restores deterrence without putting troops on the ground.

Critics note that the countries issuing the warning are also supplying weapons and refuelling support to one side of the war, so the statement can look one-sided. Aid groups worry that renewed air strikes and the seizure of Bab al-Mandab will worsen a humanitarian crisis that is already displacing more than 120,000 people, while Iran's denials mean the central accusation may never be proven publicly.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical — a textbook proxy conflict at a chokepoint
perspectives.description: Yemen follows a familiar pattern: a local civil war becomes a competition between outside powers, fought on someone else's territory. Because the Red Sea route is a chokepoint where a large share of Europe–Asia trade passes, even limited attacks there raise insurance costs and shipping prices worldwide, giving distant governments a reason to intervene that has little to do with Yemen itself.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what a settlement would require
perspectives.description: A lasting calm would require the Houthis, Yemen's government, Saudi Arabia and Iran to accept some kind of political deal, and the G7's call to return to 'the political process' points in that direction. In the meantime, watch whether the refuelling aircraft stay defensive and limited, or become the first step towards wider Western involvement — and whether shipping returns to Bab al-Mandab in normal numbers.
